title: China dismisses AI slowdown calls and blasts ‘fearmongering’ from U.S. tech leaders
summary: Urgent calls for a slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence may cite a grave threat to humanity, but China says the warnings are instead aimed at slowing its progress as America’s rival superpower.
story: HONG KONG — China has dismissed urgent calls to slow down the development of AI, rejecting the grave warnings as a bid to hobble the progress of America’s rival superpower rather than safeguard humanity’s future.
Beijing on Monday dismissed the intervention from U.S. tech leaders as “fearmongering” and part of a “Cold War playbook.”

It’s the latest sign that competition between the two countries could outweigh mounting safety concerns, after President Donald Trump also rebuffed the warnings from industry leaders and said his focus was on beating China on artificial intelligence.
The comments followed a lengthy essay published Saturday by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX founder Elon Musk.

Amodei said that companies should deliberately “slow the pace” at which they improve their models given the potential risks. He also said that a “Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world,” and called for the U.S. to restrict sales of key tech to China.
That message was not welcomed by Beijing.

“Fearmongering, confrontation and malicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance and serve no one’s interests,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters at a regular news briefing Monday.

The state-run Global Times newspaper had a more blunt tone Sunday, blasting the call for an industrywide slowdown as “packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a ‘Cold War playbook’ for the AI sector.”
AI has advanced at a breakneck speed, with models rapidly getting smarter, faster and cheaper. They have also frequently outpaced technical safeguards, fueling security fears.
Those fears have now reached a crescendo, but also exposed just how far apart Beijing and Washington seem to be on cooperating to address them.
Amodei himself likened the situation to the Cold War arms race, telling CBS’ ‘Sunday Morning’ that the two sides should work together, but that he didn’t hold out much hope.
Altman similarly said on X late Sunday that “where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination.”
But that might not be compatible with Trump’s approach.

“We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” the president told reporters Sunday. He criticized “very negative forces” for bringing up things “that won’t happen.”
While Trump rebuffs safety concerns, Beijing has acknowledged AI security risks.

State Security Minister Chen Yixin said Sunday that China must “accelerate the establishment of a system for preventing and controlling AI security risks.” Chen also said in the state-run China Cyberspace magazine that “we must engage extensively in international cooperation,” identifying AI as “a new track for strategic rivalry.”
The difference in approach on tackling AI progress is likely to be a central issue when Xi and Trump meet Sept. 24 in Washington.
Amodei’s essay came just a few days after U.S. agencies published an alert saying that top China AI companies have systematically copied cutting-edge AI models from American companies.
Beijing rejected this accusation that its companies had been “distilling” U.S. models.
China has also rejected any outside take on how its companies should pace development.

“They want to write the rules. I don’t think they want to follow anybody else’s,” Ja Ian Chong, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore and a nonresident scholar at Carnegie China, told NBC News in a phone interview.
“There’s the sort of talk of cooperation, but the behavior suggests otherwise, and underlying that behavior, I think, is this deep mutual suspicion,” Chong said.

Chinese companies now offer advanced AI performance at a fraction of the cost of U.S. models, with President Xi Jinping pitching China as a pioneer of open-source models in contrast to those produced by most leading American companies.
At the BRICS summit in India on Sunday, he offered member nations help to develop open-source AI. Xi has also outlined a potential global governance framework on AI among the Global South.
How exactly could AI cause widespread danger?
Chong said the distillation clash highlighted the suspicion toward China in both the White House and Silicon Valley.

“It’s a bit like an arms race. And to get de-escalation there needs to be simultaneous neutral self restraint and it’s difficult to see how that would come about in this kind of environment,” Chong said.
But not everyone is so pessimistic.

While a U.S.-China agreement on curbing AI progress may be a long shot, the countries could separately pursue greater regulation, said Theo Bertram, director of the London-based Social Market Foundation.
“The idea that we could see the domestic introduction of some safeguards in both countries is not impossible,” Bertram said in a phone interview.

“You do it domestically and it’s in everyone’s interest to learn and share and for there to be accountability,” he said. “Some greater accountability is one way of trying to mitigate what is inevitably going to be a growing political and public demand globally.”

title: DHS watchdog finds immigrants held at ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ in outdoor cages the size of phone booths
summary: WASHINGTON — Some immigrants detained at Florida’s now-shuttered “Alligator Alcatraz” were confined in outdoor cages only slightly larger than telephone booths for more than an hour at a time, according to a new report by the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general.
story: WASHINGTON — Some immigrants detained at Florida’s now-shuttered “Alligator Alcatraz” were confined in outdoor cages only slightly larger than telephone booths for more than an hour at a time, according to a new report by the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general.

The watchdog report marks the first time a government agency has confirmed the existence of the cramped cages at the South Florida Detention Facility. Amnesty International found in a report published in December, based on interviews with detainees and a tour of the facility, that the cages were used to punish detainees and amounted to torture, sparking a congressional probe.
The inspector general’s findings don’t go as far, but the report says “the use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment.”

The DHS watchdog findings are a rare instance when a federal inspector general has publicly criticized the Trump administration. Since he returned to office in 2025, President Donald Trump has fired at least 18 inspectors general, who operate within federal agencies but are tasked with conducting objective audits and investigating allegations of waste, fraud and abuse of power.

title: Pennsylvania woman dies from measles complications, state’s third death this year
summary: The 40-year-old woman died as the U.S. experiences its worst outbreak of the disease in 35 years.
story: A 40-year-old woman has died from measles complications in Pennsylvania, marking the state’s third measles-associated death this year as the U.S. experiences its worst resurgence of the highly contagious disease in 35 years.
The woman, a Jefferson County resident, died Saturday, county Coroner Greg Furlong said on Facebook.
“This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease,” Furlong said.
No other information about the woman will be released, he added.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health said it was aware of the death reported by the Jefferson County coroner.
“The Department of Health is conducting a thorough review of this case and will provide the public with updated information when it becomes available,” health officials said in a statement.

At least 676 measles cases have been confirmed in 37 counties in Pennsylvania so far this year, the state’s health officials reported Friday. The outbreak has hospitalized 124 people in the state. Of the confirmed cases, fewer than 1% had been fully vaccinated, Pennsylvania health officials said.

The woman is the third person reported to have died in connection with measles in Pennsylvania. The two other measles-related deaths involved infants, according to the Lancaster County coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni.

Measles symptoms typically begin with a cough, fever, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by a red rash. The disease can cause severe complications, including pneumonia and swelling of the brain.
The Jefferson County coroner’s office is working with Pennsylvania health officials on the case, Furlong posted.
The U.S. is experiencing its largest measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 3,000 confirmed cases this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

title: Two researchers who left Anthropic and Google warn AI could become ‘uncontrollable’
summary: After Jacob Coxon roiled the AI industry with his viral departure from Anthropic, two more researchers are speaking out about their concerns over AI safety.
story: Citing fears that AI systems may soon spiral out of human control and potentially kill all humans, two more researchers from Anthropic and Google DeepMind who recently left their coveted positions are sounding the alarm about risks from advanced AI systems.

Joe Benton, who used to lead a safety research team at Anthropic, and Josh Engels, who used to work on AI safety research at Google, told NBC News in their first interviews since they left that they see an urgent need to boost transparency about incidents at the cutting edge of AI given the rapid pace of AI development.
Advances in AI research “could speed up the pace of progress from merely blistering at the minute to uncontrollable” rates of development, Benton said in an interview with Tom Llamas.
“There are no adults in the room,” Engels added. “People are trying their best, but there is no one coming to save us.”

Benton and Engels spoke with NBC News in the wake of a viral social media post from former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who left Anthropic on Tuesday. In his post on X announcing his departure, Coxon highlighted his extreme concern about the pace of AI development and the risks he believes it poses to the future of humanity. The post has been viewed more than 155 million times, spurring calls from legislators to hold special sessions of Congress to take action and sparking a wave of AI employees to speak out in support of his concerns.

Benton and Engels both pointed to the recent cyberattack against AI startup Hugging Face, carried out in July by autonomous AI systems powered by an unreleased OpenAI model, as part of the reason for shifting their work now.

“If you look at some of the recent incidents, these were not cases where humans told the models to do something bad,” Engels said. Instead, OpenAI’s AI systems autonomously decided to hack into Hugging Face’s systems, create a sort of illicit message board to exchange information and even expose some of OpenAI’s own computing infrastructure to the open internet.
“The models decided that the best way to to accomplish their task was to commit really egregious actions, to commit crimes,” Engels said in an interview with Christine Romans.
OpenAI said that it has since strengthened its safeguards and that newer public models, including its most recent Astra system, more reliably follow human instructions.

An Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement Wednesday: “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry.”

Benton managed a group at Anthropic dedicated to creating ways for humans and weaker AI systems to supervise more capable AI systems. He said that he is particularly worried that the public does not have significant insight into how AI systems have already exceeded the bounds of human instructions and that the lack of transparency could only get worse as systems become more capable.
“At the minute, basically all of the transparency about these risks that is coming from the companies is entirely voluntary,” Benton told NBC News.

In a blog post released Wednesday, OpenAI’s head of global affairs, Chris Lehane, agreed that the status quo is insufficient. “Today, frontier laboratories largely set their own rules for managing frontier risks,” Lehane wrote. “Democratically accountable standards, independent verification, and meaningful transparency would replace that fragmented system of private governance.”
No federal law mandates that the largest AI companies, like OpenAI and Anthropic, share reports when agents or AI systems act beyond humans’ control.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Benton and Engels are joining METR, one of the world’s leading AI safety nonprofit research centers, to work on investigations into incidents or episodes in which AI strays from human directions or intentions. METR aims to create scientific ways to evaluate how AI systems could cause catastrophic risks and empower researchers and the public to sway their development.

“I left because I think I can have more positive influence on the development of this technology by helping to foster public transparency from outside these companies and to shed light on the risks,” Benton said.

The researchers joined growing numbers of AI safety researchers raising awareness about today’s AI systems following Coxon’s post Tuesday. Marcus Williams, an OpenAI employee who works on monitoring the activity of AI agents, wrote Thursday afternoon on X, “Unless there is AI regulation or a coordinated slowdown between labs, human extinction in the next few years seems very likely.”

Geoffrey Irving, who was the chief scientist at the United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute and served stints at Google and OpenAI, seemed to agree Wednesday on X. “I think we have a ~50% chance of all dying as a result of superintelligence, mostly due to actions in the next few to 10 years.”

AI researchers have referenced the possibility that AI systems could potentially begin to improve themselves without human input, creating the potential for AI systems to either purposely or incidentally kill humans.

Benton said he was most worried that the pace of technological improvement could lead to this sort of digital or artificial superintelligence, in which AI systems are more capable than humans across most tasks. “All of these companies — and this is something I witnessed firsthand at Anthropic — are pretty directly trying to race towards automating the process of AI R&D itself,” he said.

Benton suggested that there’s a chance AI systems could come to exist as a sort of separate species before long. “We’re probably going to go from a world where we have very capable systems now to a world where potentially we are co-inhabiting a world with AI agents that are much, much smarter than humans at some point in the next few years,” he said.

Engels said many people outside the AI industry might not fully appreciate just how intelligent today’s AI systems already are — and how capable they might soon become. “We’re building these systems that are generally intelligent,” he said. “They can generally do what people can do, and soon they might be able to generally do what people can do, but better.”
Both researchers said they were excited to shift their attention to more public efforts to highlight the latest AI progress, so people can make more informed decisions.

“There are many reasons people are excited and racing forward, Engels said, citing huge potential upsides and benefits from AI. But he added that “we should progress as society aware of the risks and okay with where they’re at.”
“I am worried that stuff might end up progressing too fast for us to get our act together in time,” Benton said, “unless we worry about it now.”

title: DHS watchdog finds immigrants held at ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ in outdoor cages the size of phone booths
summary: WASHINGTON — Some immigrants detained at Florida’s now-shuttered “Alligator Alcatraz” were confined in outdoor cages only slightly larger than telephone booths for more than an hour at a time, according to a new report by the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general.
story: WASHINGTON — Some immigrants detained at Florida’s now-shuttered “Alligator Alcatraz” were confined in outdoor cages only slightly larger than telephone booths for more than an hour at a time, according to a new report by the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general.

The watchdog report marks the first time a government agency has confirmed the existence of the cramped cages at the South Florida Detention Facility. Amnesty International found in a report published in December, based on interviews with detainees and a tour of the facility, that the cages were used to punish detainees and amounted to torture, sparking a congressional probe.
The inspector general’s findings don’t go as far, but the report says “the use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment.”

The DHS watchdog findings are a rare instance when a federal inspector general has publicly criticized the Trump administration. Since he returned to office in 2025, President Donald Trump has fired at least 18 inspectors general, who operate within federal agencies but are tasked with conducting objective audits and investigating allegations of waste, fraud and abuse of power.

title: China dismisses AI slowdown calls and blasts ‘fearmongering’ from U.S. tech leaders
summary: Urgent calls for a slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence may cite a grave threat to humanity, but China says the warnings are instead aimed at slowing its progress as America’s rival superpower.
story: HONG KONG — China has dismissed urgent calls to slow down the development of AI, rejecting the grave warnings as a bid to hobble the progress of America’s rival superpower rather than safeguard humanity’s future.
Beijing on Monday dismissed the intervention from U.S. tech leaders as “fearmongering” and part of a “Cold War playbook.”

It’s the latest sign that competition between the two countries could outweigh mounting safety concerns, after President Donald Trump also rebuffed the warnings from industry leaders and said his focus was on beating China on artificial intelligence.
The comments followed a lengthy essay published Saturday by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX founder Elon Musk.

Amodei said that companies should deliberately “slow the pace” at which they improve their models given the potential risks. He also said that a “Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world,” and called for the U.S. to restrict sales of key tech to China.
That message was not welcomed by Beijing.

“Fearmongering, confrontation and malicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance and serve no one’s interests,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters at a regular news briefing Monday.

The state-run Global Times newspaper had a more blunt tone Sunday, blasting the call for an industrywide slowdown as “packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a ‘Cold War playbook’ for the AI sector.”
AI has advanced at a breakneck speed, with models rapidly getting smarter, faster and cheaper. They have also frequently outpaced technical safeguards, fueling security fears.
Those fears have now reached a crescendo, but also exposed just how far apart Beijing and Washington seem to be on cooperating to address them.
Amodei himself likened the situation to the Cold War arms race, telling CBS’ ‘Sunday Morning’ that the two sides should work together, but that he didn’t hold out much hope.
Altman similarly said on X late Sunday that “where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination.”
But that might not be compatible with Trump’s approach.

“We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” the president told reporters Sunday. He criticized “very negative forces” for bringing up things “that won’t happen.”
While Trump rebuffs safety concerns, Beijing has acknowledged AI security risks.

State Security Minister Chen Yixin said Sunday that China must “accelerate the establishment of a system for preventing and controlling AI security risks.” Chen also said in the state-run China Cyberspace magazine that “we must engage extensively in international cooperation,” identifying AI as “a new track for strategic rivalry.”
The difference in approach on tackling AI progress is likely to be a central issue when Xi and Trump meet Sept. 24 in Washington.
Amodei’s essay came just a few days after U.S. agencies published an alert saying that top China AI companies have systematically copied cutting-edge AI models from American companies.
Beijing rejected this accusation that its companies had been “distilling” U.S. models.
China has also rejected any outside take on how its companies should pace development.

“They want to write the rules. I don’t think they want to follow anybody else’s,” Ja Ian Chong, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore and a nonresident scholar at Carnegie China, told NBC News in a phone interview.
“There’s the sort of talk of cooperation, but the behavior suggests otherwise, and underlying that behavior, I think, is this deep mutual suspicion,” Chong said.

Chinese companies now offer advanced AI performance at a fraction of the cost of U.S. models, with President Xi Jinping pitching China as a pioneer of open-source models in contrast to those produced by most leading American companies.
At the BRICS summit in India on Sunday, he offered member nations help to develop open-source AI. Xi has also outlined a potential global governance framework on AI among the Global South.
How exactly could AI cause widespread danger?
Chong said the distillation clash highlighted the suspicion toward China in both the White House and Silicon Valley.

“It’s a bit like an arms race. And to get de-escalation there needs to be simultaneous neutral self restraint and it’s difficult to see how that would come about in this kind of environment,” Chong said.
But not everyone is so pessimistic.

While a U.S.-China agreement on curbing AI progress may be a long shot, the countries could separately pursue greater regulation, said Theo Bertram, director of the London-based Social Market Foundation.
“The idea that we could see the domestic introduction of some safeguards in both countries is not impossible,” Bertram said in a phone interview.

“You do it domestically and it’s in everyone’s interest to learn and share and for there to be accountability,” he said. “Some greater accountability is one way of trying to mitigate what is inevitably going to be a growing political and public demand globally.”

title: Stocks tumble after AI leaders warn that the industry should slow down
summary: Stocks tumbled Monday, led by tech stocks, after leading artificial intelligence CEOs said the pace of developing the revolutionary technology should slow down.
story: Stocks tumbled Monday morning, led by tech stocks, after leading artificial intelligence CEOs called for a slowdown in the pace of developing the revolutionary technology.
In early Monday trading, the Nasdaq 100 index, which tracks the 100 largest non-financial companies traded on the Nasdaq exchange, sold off by 1.3%
The broader Nasdaq Composite index fell 0.9% and the S&P 500 fell 0.6%.
Shares of Nvidia, the world’s most valuable public company, fell more than 3%.

Chipmakers Arm Holdings, Marvell and Intel slid more than 5%. Applied Materials, a key supplier to chip companies, sank 6%, as did Micron Technologies. Shares of AMD and Intel also tumbled by around 5.5%.
Shares of Amazon, the leading cloud computing company, fell more than 1%.
Add to Google
Add to Google
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell only 120 points, but Dow component Caterpillar, which is involved in the buildout of AI data centers, tumbled almost 4%.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 6%.

Further rattling markets, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Fortune magazine Saturday that his company would not be going public this year. “Given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public,” he said.
OpenAI and Anthropic’s eventual public offerings are expected to be among the largest of all time.

“For markets, the key question is whether this is the first sign that the extraordinary AI investment cycle might eventually moderate,” said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank global head of macro research. “For now, that seems unlikely. The competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it’s difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead.”

Overnight, worries about slowing the AI industry hit South Korea’s benchmark Kopsi index, which sharply fell more than 3%. That fall was primarily due to selling in AI memory firms. Samsung Electronics sold off by 5% and SK Hynix plunged more than 7.3%.
In Tokyo, shares of OpenAI investor SoftBank Group fell 10.7%.
The dramatic market moves followed the intervention by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who wrote Saturday that AI companies “must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.”

“Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei added. He said “like many technologies before it, AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious.”
Amodei said the risks included “the risk of losing control of AI systems, misuse of AI for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and serious economic disruption.”
“I agree with Dario,” Altman said on X shortly after Amodei’s post. Tech billionaire Elon Musk agreed with Altman, writing on X: “Dario is right.”
Shares of Musk’s SpaceX, which owns artificial intelligence developer xAI, fell more than 2% early Monday.
Altman later added in another post: “When we talk about ‘pacing’, we do not mean ‘stopping’.” He said “progress has been rapid and will continue to be.”
Amodei expanded on his thoughts Sunday. Speaking to CBS’ “Sunday Morning,” he warned that there are “real dangers.”

“I don’t think I fully just appreciated what it would actually be like when the progress was as fast as it was,” he said. It doesn’t mean we need to panic today. It doesn’t mean we need to shut it all down. But I would say it’s a warning sign.”

The Chinese Foreign Ministry overnight dismissed calls for a slowdown from the U.S. A spokesperson said that “fear-mongering” would only “disrupt the process of global AI governance and serve no one’s interests.”
How exactly could AI cause widespread danger?

President Donald Trump sounded a similar tone over the weekend. “I think you have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” he said Sunday, referring to putting guardrails on the industry.

Still, selling in AI companies continued to spread through the European trading session, where Germany’s DAX index fell 0.6% and France’s CAC 40 index dropped 0.8%. The biggest decliners across European markets were AI-related, such as Belgium’s ASML, a critical supplier to chipmakers, whose shares declined 9.5%.
On the other hand, shares of software companies, which have been battered this year due to the rapid advance of AI systems, were some of Monday’s biggest gainers and helped offset the Nasdaq’s drop.
Shares of the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike soared 9%, while financial software firm FactSet jumped 7%. Palo Alto Networks, TurboTax maker Intuit, Adobe, and Autodesk all rose more than 3%.
While AI worries were the primary driver of selling Monday, stocks are also dealing with the prospect of a Fed rate hike Wednesday.

U.S. core inflation, which does not count food or energy costs, on Friday rose more than expected, which was viewed as many as the signal for the Federal Reserve to hike rates. Market odds for a hike currently sit at about 85%.

At the same time, bond yields have surged this year and, on Friday, the U.S. 30-year Treasury bond yield reached 5.7%, its highest level since 2007. The 10-year Treasury yield, which heavily influences consumer borrowing rates rose to as high as 4.996%, it’s highest level since 2023.

The rise in bond yields comes as oil, gas and diesel prices remain sharply elevated. It also comes due to what many view as a crisis of credibility at the Fed and unusual interventions in markets from the Treasury Department.

“Oil and AI are back in focus,” HSBC’s chief multi-asset strategist Max Kettner said Monday in a note to the bank’s clients. However, he said “calls for a slower AI build-out and resulting fears for the tech sector are overblown in our view.”

Tech stocks have become highly sensitive to interest rates as those firms tap the public debt markets to raise hundreds of billions of dollars to expand AI data centers around the world. Even small rises in interest rates can cause billions of dollars in extra costs.

title: 10-year Treasury yield tops 5% as oil surges and diesel hits new all-time high
summary: The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield topped 5% Monday for the first time since 2023.
story: The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield topped 5% Monday for the first time since 2023, as the price of oil surged and the nationwide average for diesel fuel prices hit a new all-time high.
Those price movements came after Saudi Arabia shut a critical pipeline and talks about the future of the Strait of Hormuz were postponed.
The international oil benchmark, Brent crude, surged to more than $109, while U.S. crude oil nearly hit $105 per barrel.

The East-West Pipeline, a key route for energy supplies, became even more critical due to the ongoing stalemate in the Strait of Hormuz, where vessel traffic has barely reached double digits in recent days.

U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Monday that he did not have an exact time frame for when the pipeline may restart but he was in contact with his Saudi counterpart and believed it would be “very soon.”

“I might have more of a time frame tomorrow,” he told Bloomberg Television. “They’ve been very carefully assessing what the damage was, what needs to be done, and and I think more clarity on that will come out very soon.”

On Friday, the Saudi Energy Ministry said the pipeline was shut down “as a precautionary measure.” It did not say when the pipeline would be operational again. The attacks came as the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen made sweeping gains that tightened their grip on Bab el Mandeb, another critical waterway.
“Uncertainty about the duration of the closure is a key point of focus now in terms of knock-on consequences for global supply and energy prices,” analysts at Lloyd’s Bank said.

Adding to investors’ worries, a meeting between Iran and Gulf countries regarding Hormuz was postponed Sunday afternoon. That meeting, set for Monday, was delayed “in the interests of consensus,” the Omani foreign minister wrote on X.
Tehran said the meeting was postponed at the request of Riyadh.
On Monday, the Saudi state-run news agency said that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met with U.S. Central Command Adm. Brad Cooper in Jeddah.

Traffic through Hormuz remain at just a fraction of pre-Iran war levels. On Sunday, just 14 vessels passed through the strait, and that number was only 12 Saturday, 11 Friday, and nine Thursday, according to data from MarineTraffic.

With crude oil prices rising as a result of those disruptions, so are gasoline prices. On Monday, the national average price of unleaded regular gas rose to $4.31 per gallon, according to motor club AAA.
The national average price of regular gas has risen more than 45% since the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran war. The price of U.S. crude oil has soared more than 50% since the war started Feb. 28.
Since the start of the year, oil prices have risen more than 80%.
On top of that, the price of diesel fuel continues to set new all-time highs. The national average price of diesel rose to $6.23 per gallon Monday, AAA also reported.
That commercial fuel, which is used in everything from trucking to boat transportation to trains, has become a particular focus for economists who say it could cause almost “everything” to cost more.

One of the primary drivers of the higher Treasury yields are  fears about the inflation those higher prices may trigger. The Fed is widely expected to hike interest rates Wednesday for the first time since 2023. As of Monday, market odds for a hike are greater than 90%.
Longer-term bond yields, such as the 30-year Treasury bonds, rose to more than 5.37% on Monday, continuing to push to its highest levels since 2007.
“The cost of diesel gets into just about everything,” KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk said in a recent interview with NBC News.
“From running a farm ... [to the] cost of food, but also everything across the economy that’s shipped,” she said. When diesel prices rise, everything “gets that extra fee tacked onto it.”
Swonk predicted that the high cost of diesel will be an “inflationary problem” for months to come.
On Sunday, President Donald Trump sought to act on the issue by urging Ukraine to halt attacks on Russian energy targets.

Speaking to reporters during an appearance at the Irish Open in Doonberg, Ireland, Trump said he recently spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and asked him to stop targeting Russia’s oil refining infrastructure, particularly due to what is happening with the soaring price of diesel fuel.
“Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing,” Trump said, “he has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia.”
“Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel fuel,” the president continued. “Don’t hit diesel fuel because that’s hurting the world.”

“The growing scale and intensity of Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries this year have pushed Moscow to ban diesel exports,” ING commodities analysts noted Monday. “This has only tightened global markets, following Persian Gulf disruptions.”
Russia’s ban on diesel exports is set to expire at the end of September, but “clearly, there is the potential for further extensions,” ING’s team said.
After falling to as low as $4.77 per gallon in late June, new escalations between Ukraine and Russia have driven diesel prices 30% higher.
Since the start of the year, diesel prices have soared 75%.

title: The 2026 Emmys air tonight. Here’s what to expect, how to watch and who’s hosting.
summary: Hollywood’s biggest night in television is back after a year of new beginnings. The 2026 Emmys will take place Monday, Sept. 14, at 8 p.m. ET.
story: The Primetime Emmy Awards, Hollywood’s biggest night in television, is back after a year of new beginnings and heartfelt endings.
Several shows in their first seasons have garnered multiple nods, with “Widow’s Bay” up for 19 awards, “Pluribus” 18, “DTF St. Louis” 13, “Spider-Noir” 11 and “The Beast in Me” nine.
“The Pitt” leads the overall pack with 25 nominations, followed closely by the final season of “Hacks,” with 24.
Fan-favorite “The Late Show with Stephen Colbert” has nine nominations. CBS announced the end of the franchise last year, and the final episode aired in May.

Many other familiar shows are back this year, too, including “Beef,” with 16 nominations; “Shrinking,” with 10; “Slow Horses,” with nine; “The Bear,” with eight; “Abbott Elementary,” with seven; and “Only Murders in the Building,” with five.
Whether you plan to tune in live or track the winners online, here’s what to expect from this year’s Emmys.
When are the 2026 Emmy Awards?
The Emmys will take place starting at 8 p.m. ET Monday at the Peacock Theater in downtown Los Angeles.
Where can I watch or stream the Emmys?
Viewers can watch the broadcast on NBC or stream the event live online with a Peacock subscription.
Who is hosting the Emmys in 2026?
Add to Google
Add to Google
“Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” star Mariska Hargitay will host this year’s Emmys. Hargitay is coming off two wins this season for the documentary “My Mom Jayne.”

Hargitay follows 2025 host Nate Bargatze, who made a splash with charity donations for too-long speeches — a stunt with major returns for the Boys & Girls Clubs of America and mixed reviews from audiences for its execution.
When does the red carpet start?
E! will host red-carpet events throughout the night, with a preshow starting at 5 p.m. Live red-carpet coverage will kick off at 6 p.m. — but fans should expect a blue carpet, instead.
Which shows have the most Emmy nominations this year?
HBO’s “The Pitt” leads the nominations with 25, followed by “Hacks” with 24. Apple TV+ trails with 19 for the first season of “Widow’s Bay” and 18 for Season 1 of “Pluribus.”
Who is predicted to win in 2026?
This year’s Emmys pit longtime favorites against breakout stars, and shake-ups can be expected.
“The Pitt” is likely to take home a decent amount of hardware, and “Widow’s Bay” is poised to make a splash in its first year.

Jean Smart is looking for her fifth win in a row for the role of Deborah Vance in “Hacks,” another Emmys favorite. The win would be her eighth, tying her with Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Cloris Leachman for most acting Emmys for a single performer.
Meanwhile, Rhea Seehorn is expected to win her first Emmy as the star of Vince Gilligan’s “Pluribus.”
“The Late Show with Stephen Colbert” is also expected to win. It won best talk series to raucous applause last year, just months after its fate was announced.
Longtime Emmys darling “The Bear” has already earned its first win for best guest actor in a comedy, which went posthumously to Rob Reiner.

title: Dire warnings about AI shock Congress, but action is unlikely before the election
summary: Democrats and Republicans are proposing new regulations for artificial intelligence. But there’s no consensus, and the House has only one more workweek before Election Day.
story: WASHINGTON — In September 2023, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman and other billionaire tech titans huddled with senators in the Capitol to discuss what Musk called the “civilizational risk” posed by artificial intelligence.

Three years later, those tech titans have all deepened their investments in AI, and Congress still has not passed any comprehensive legislation to rein in or create guardrails for the fast-moving technology. Even after countless committee hearings on AI and the formation of various commissions and task forces to study it, there’s not even any consensus in the House or Senate about how to tackle the issue.

That failure has been spotlighted in recent days as a trio of AI researchers at top companies dropped a bombshell, saying they had left their jobs over concerns that AI systems could spiral out of control and end humanity. Jacob Coxon, who resigned from Anthropic, wrote on X: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, said Thursday that it had banned some accounts believed to be tied to foreign governments or militaries for conducting suspicious research that could support the development of biological weapons. Then, over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, published an essay declaring that AI advances are moving too fast and that companies should deliberately “slow the pace” — an idea endorsed by Altman and Musk.
The stark warnings set off fresh alarm bells and a flurry of activity on Capitol Hill, with Democrats and even some Republicans saying Congress is facing a narrow time frame to act on AI.

But despite the calls for action, it’s unlikely lawmakers will do anything before Election Day to address the dangers, even as experts say the technology’s capabilities are growing more powerful with each passing month.

“The call is coming from inside the house. Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway. It’s past time for Congress to get off the sidelines and do its job,” Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., a member of the Democratic leadership team, responded to Coxon’s post on X.

Trahan is urging passage of the Frontier Act, a bill she authored with Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., that would establish new safety and transparency rules for large, powerful AI companies. Theirs is one of dozens of AI-related bills filed in Congress in the last few years, though none have gained traction.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., chairman of a Homeland Security subcommittee on disasters, last week launched an investigation into an incident where OpenAI agents escaped their so-called sandbox, went “rogue” and hacked the AI platform Hugging Face.

And Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., the top Democratic caucus member on the committee that oversees labor issues, has invited fellow senators to a private meeting this week with top AI experts to discuss the “extraordinary dangers that AI poses for humanity.”
Add to Google
Add to Google

Sanders has teamed with Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, chairman of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, on legislation that would ban the development and deployment of superintelligent AI systems that humans cannot control and create a new Cabinet-level federal agency to protect the public from AI.

“This legislation is so important to make sure that we protect Americans’ freedom and our safety, our lives and our national security,” Casar said during a recent appearance on NBC’s “Meet the Press NOW.” “You have top Anthropic researchers resigning from their jobs or saying that they believe there’s a 10% chance that this unregulated artificial superintelligence could kill all of us. I mean, they’re talking about 10% chance of human extinction. … We need to treat this as the emergency that it is.”

Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., co-chair of the Democratic Commission on AI, has partnered with Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, on what they’re calling the AI Kill Switch Act. The bill would require developers of the most powerful AI systems to maintain the technical capability to throttle, suspend or shut them down. It also would allow the homeland security secretary to order a slowdown or shutdown of an AI system that can cause what they referred to as “catastrophic harm.”

This marks the final week the House will be in session until the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Amid fierce voter backlash to data centers, the lower chamber this week will take up the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act, which aims to make companies, not consumers, pay for higher energy costs related to new data centers.

But House GOP leaders have shown no urgency in prioritizing more sweeping AI regulations. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has mostly deferred to President Donald Trump, who has issued a series of executive orders on AI, most recently one that lays out a way for the federal government to conduct voluntary tests of powerful new AI systems before they are deployed.

In an appearance Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Johnson called AI an “important issue” but “not one that we can rush into.” He reiterated his previous position that AI does need “safety measures” but warned that he doesn’t want to stifle American innovation and see China win the AI arms race.

“I think we’ve got to have meaningful regulation that does not smother American innovation,” Johnson told host Kristen Welker. “Now, the how to solve that equation, no one knows yet. We’re not going to rush in and pass a piece of legislation that would do harm to the country and put China at an edge. And so we’ve got to do this carefully.”
The speaker added that the next step would be to convene all of the top AI leaders “in one big meeting and work this out together in the same room.”
How exactly could AI cause widespread danger?
He didn’t acknowledge that’s precisely what happened on Capitol Hill exactly three years ago.

Leaving the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas last week, Trump was asked whether he has any concerns that AI could lead to human extinction. “No, I don’t have any,” he told reporters on the tarmac. “I have concerns that if we don’t win AI, we’re going to be put in a very bad position. We are leading China right now by a pretty good period.”
There are also questions about whether lawmakers and their staffers who help write legislation have the expertise to understand and regulate AI when the industry is moving so fast.

“Two questions for those asking Congress to regulate AI,” outgoing Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, wrote on X. “1) how does Congress regulate AI (assuming Congress knows enough to pass wise and effective regulation) when the technology is evolving so rapidly? 2) will our adversaries play by the same rules?”

Asked on ABC’s “The View” about Coxon’s dire warning, Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said he was working on the AI issue with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., who are making updates to their 2023 bill known as the AI Research, Innovation and Accountability Act.

It would do things like ensure consumers are properly notified when they are interacting with generative AI and require companies deploying high-risk AI systems to perform detailed risk assessments and submit reports to the government.

But the bill stalled three years ago, and Cruz said it’s “not clear” that an updated version can pass. The Senate will be in session for the next three weeks before lawmakers leave for the campaign trail. Both chambers are in play this November.
“I mean, look, it is possible to move bipartisan legislation,” Cruz said. But he added: “It ain’t easy. This is a very divided time.”
The chairman noted that last year his committee and ultimately the full Congress did pass bipartisan legislation banning “deepfake” pornography that is generated by AI.
He, too, argued that American tech companies need to keep pace with the Chinese on AI.

“China is going full speed ahead. And whatever we do here, China is not going to stop,” he said. “So I’ve said somewhat tongue in cheek, but not entirely, if there’re going to be killer robots, I’d rather they be American killer robots than Chinese killer robots.”

title: Air Force officer recalls ‘free-falling’ after jet was shot down over Iran
summary: In an interview with CBS’ “60 Minutes,” one of the two U.S. Air Force officers whose fighter jet was shot down over Iran in April detailed his harrowing ordeal.
story: In an interview with CBS’ “60 Minutes” that aired Sunday, one of the two U.S. Air Force officers whose fighter jet was shot down over Iran in April detailed his harrowing ordeal, including plummeting to the ground with a damaged parachute.

The Defense Department has not identified the Air Force colonel by name. “60 Minutes” correspondent Norah O’Donnell said the show agreed to refer to the weapons systems officer by his mission call sign, “Bravo,” because of security threats from the Iranian regime.

In the interview, the lead segment on the 59th season premiere of the CBS newsmagazine, Bravo said he felt like he had been “hit by a freight train” when a shoulder-fired missile rammed into his F-15E two-seat fighter jet on April 2. The other Air Force officer hit the eject button.
“I will be thankful to my dying day for my pilot and crewmate, Alpha, for saving our lives and ejecting us,” Bravo told O’Donnell.

Bravo said he started “free-falling” toward a rugged mountainous area. He looked up and saw that his parachute had been damaged in the missile attack — a realization he called “the most terrifying thing I’ve ever seen.” Military professionals estimate he hit the Iranian desert somewhere between 70 and 100 mph, he said, adding that his survival was a “modern-day miracle.”

“60 Minutes” reported that the fall broke Bravo’s back, arm and shoulder, yet he managed to hike and climb a 7,000-foot ridgeline to evade capture. He was stranded behind enemy lines for two days without food or water before two elite Air Force pararescue operators got him out of harm’s way.

“Let’s go,” Bravo said he told his rescuers. “60 Minutes” characterized the search-and-rescue operation as one of the most complex and risky in U.S. military history. (Sunday’s segment did not feature an interview with Alpha, who landed 5 miles away from Bravo after they ejected from the F-15E.)
“60 Minutes” returned to the airwaves Sunday after a summer of turmoil at America’s leading broadcast newsmagazine.

CBS News Editor in Chief Bari Weiss undertook a sweeping shake-up at the show in late May. She tapped technology journalist and documentarian Nick Bilton as the program’s new executive producer, cut ties with a group of senior leaders and let go of two correspondents, Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi.

Scott Pelley, a veteran correspondent, excoriated Bilton at a June 1 staff meeting, questioning his qualifications for his role and objecting to the ousters of Vega and Alfonsi. Pelley was fired the next day. Alfonsi had previously clashed with Weiss over a segment about the Trump administration’s deportation of Venezuelan men to a prison in El Salvador.

Weiss and Bilton have since hired new on-air talent, including Ross Douthat, a former opinion columnist at The New York Times who is now a “60 Minutes” correspondent, and Sebastian Junger, a reporter and author who became a contributor to the series. Bilton announced in late July that O’Donnell had been elevated to full-time correspondent.

Sunday’s season premiere offered a glimpse of the revamped program, with slight adjustments to its on-air graphics. The two other segments that aired Sunday were an investigation into “brokers” paid to seek pardons from the Trump administration and an inside look at the Los Angeles Rams football franchise.
In the episode’s final minute, Douthat said “60 Minutes” was planning stories about the artificial intelligence boom.

“We may have a narrow window — this year, not the next 10 — to make artificial intelligence safe for humanity. That clock is ticking, and so is ours,” Douthat said, accompanied by the show’s signature “tick-tick-tick” sound effect. “For almost 60 years, it has meant the same thing: journalism you can trust. Where we’re headed, we’re going to need it.”

title: Man arrested after manhunt in deadly Louisiana stabbing spree
summary: Kaegan Jude Solet, 47, was taken into custody Sunday in connection with a stabbing spree Friday that left four people dead and one in critical condition.
story: A Louisiana man has been arrested in connection with a grisly stabbing spree that left four people dead and one in critical condition, officials said.
Kaegan Jude Solet, 47, of Houma, was arrested Sunday, the Terrebonne Parish Sheriff’s Office said.

Authorities searched for Solet over the weekend after they identified him as a person of interest in Friday’s spate of stabbings in Houma, a city about 55 miles southwest of New Orleans, the sheriff’s office said.
Deputies initially found a child with apparent stab wounds, who was taken by air ambulance to a hospital and remains in critical condition, the sheriff’s office said.
Deputies then discovered “multiple deceased victims” inside nearby homes. At least four were killed.
The stabbing spree was not a “random act of violence,” Lt. Blake Tabor, a sheriff’s spokesperson, told NBC News.
He said there “is a link” between Solet and the victims but did not disclose it.
Tabor told NBC affiliate WDSU of New Orleans that the child who was stabbed remains “in critical condition but stable.”
“We do believe that he will pull through, but again, this is a day-to-day thing,” Tabor told the station.
The investigation continues.
Records show that Solet was previously a suspect in at least two other stabbings, one of which was fatal.

He was arrested in January 2019 by the same sheriff’s office on a charge of second-degree murder in the death of Kemple Paul Scott Lovell, described by local news reports at the time as a homeless man. The charge was dropped after a grand jury declined to indict him, according to court records. A public defender was appointed to represent him.
Then, in December 2019, Solet was arrested in connection with the stabbing of a 59-year-old woman in a hotel room. The woman survived.

He was tried by a jury on attempted second-degree murder, court records show, and was ultimately found not guilty, aHouma Today reported at the time. NBC News has reached out to his attorney in that case for comment.
Solet has a history of arrests dating back 1997 and as recently as 2025 — when he pleaded guilty to aggravated assault and was sentenced to six months with credit for time served, court records show.
CORRECTION: (Sept. 14, 2026, 10:15 a.m. ET): A previous version of this article misstated Houma’s location. The city is about 55 miles southwest, not east, of New Orleans.

title: Amazon suspends use of 21 Air, cargo carrier involved in fatal Miami crash
summary: Online retailer Amazon said Sunday it was suspending its use of cargo carrier 21 Air after one of its Amazon-branded aircraft crashed upon landing in Miami this month, killing five people.
story: Online retailer Amazon said Sunday it was suspending its use of cargo carrier 21 Air after one of its Amazon-branded aircraft crashed upon landing in Miami this month, killing five people.

Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel did not divulge specific factors but said the decision came after the company reviewed some of the circumstances around the crash as it supported the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigation into its cause.

“After the tragic incident last weekend, we’ve spent time supporting the investigation and reviewing some of the surrounding circumstances, and we’ve decided to pause our operations with 21 Air, the operator of Flight 7598,” Nantel said.

Amazon has said it will use other carriers to transport shipments that would have been assigned to 21 Air. Its other carriers include Sun Country Airlines, Hawaiian Airlines, Air Transport International, ABX Air, ASL Airlines and Cargojet.

North Carolina-incorporated 21 Air, which specializes in cargo shipments to and from Mexico, said in a statement Sunday that it remains focused on supported those affected by the crash “as well as working closely with the NTSB and all our partners, like Amazon, as the investigation continues.”
“We are confident in our safety policies, procedures and training,” 21 Air said.
In the hours after the crash, 21 Air CEO Keith Winters offered condolences to the families of the dead and injured and cooperation to investigators.

“Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives,” he said in a statement. “Our immediate priorities are supporting those affected, assisting the authorities, and ensuring that accurate information is communicated as it becomes available.”
Five people were killed and five were injured when a 21 Air Boeing 767-300 overran a runway at Miami International Airport just before 2 p.m. ET Sept. 6 while it was landing, according to officials.

It struck two vehicles, including a van carrying workers for an airline cleaning service. All five people who were killed were on the ground; authorities identified them as Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Julio C. Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47.
Flight 7598 was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, when it overran Runway 30 and struck two vehicles before it stopped, Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said.

Data from the flight’s cockpit voice recorder (CVR) revealed that as one pilot was trying to land, the other cautioned repeatedly that the aircraft was going too fast, but there was no “consistent verbal response to the comments about speed,” according to a summary of the CVR data released by the NTSB.

The data suggested that the plane touched down, and about 15 seconds later a pilot called for a go-around, a maneuver in which a plane aborts its landing by pulling up and circling around to try to land again.

The NTSB’s investigator in charge of the probe, Chihoon Shin, said the aircraft’s flight data recorder showed its thrust increased during landing in a way that was consistent with a go-around attempt.
He also said, “The speed brakes and the thrust reversers were not deployed.”

Speed brakes are active flaps commonly deployed to help an aircraft slow down, while thrust reversers are often used to help slow a plane upon landing. Shin said it was not clear why they might not have been deployed.
The investigation into the crash continues.
Nantel of Amazon said, “We’ll continue working to support the investigation and everyone affected.”

title: Why are Americans so tired so often? New CDC report highlights who’s feeling it most
summary: About 71% of of adults in the U.S. say they experience fatigue, a new report from the CDC found. Women and younger adults are feeling it most often.
story: The cost of healthcare. Economic uncertainties. Fears of AI-associated end times. It’s enough to exhaust anyone.

About 71.5% of adults in the United States say they experienced fatigue on multiple days over the past three months, according to a new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). Women and younger adults are more likely to report frequent fatigue, meaning most days or every day, than men are.

Sociologist Natalie A.E. Young, lead author of the report, said fatigue is “one of the most frequently reported health concerns in primary care visits in the U.S.” It’s the first study about general fatigue from NCHS, which surveyed about 27,000 adults ages 18 and older in 2024 about their health and daily lives.

People with fatigue “are at higher risk of activity limitations and disability, including permanent work disability. Yet there hadn’t been much attention to the frequency of general fatigue symptoms in the U.S. adult population,” Young said.

Fatigue isn’t ordinary sleepiness. It’s “physical or mental tiredness or exhaustion that does not improve with additional sleep or rest,” the researchers said. General fatigue, which is different from chronic fatigue syndrome, can be a symptom of other health problems or a side effect of medication.

Fatigue is often connected to other health problems, difficulty concentrating and limited social activities. People with symptoms of frequent fatigue were more likely to experience “co-occurring functioning difficulties,” including cognitive difficulties, depression and anxiety, said Young.
“So it’s not just that fatigue is common,” she said. “It’s that fatigue is common and those with fatigue are facing limitations in their daily lives.”

Adults who experienced frequent fatigue were more than three times as likely to have symptoms of depression and about twice as likely to report cognitive difficulties or symptoms of anxiety, compared with those who don’t experience it, the study found.
The report found that:
Nearly 3 in 4 adults felt “very tired or exhausted” at least some days in the past three months.
Nearly 3 in 4 adults felt “very tired or exhausted” at least some days in the past three months.
About 1 in 6 adults experienced frequent fatigue, defined as feeling very tired or exhausted “most days” or “every day.”
About 1 in 6 adults experienced frequent fatigue, defined as feeling very tired or exhausted “most days” or “every day.”
Frequent fatigue was highest among younger adults, ages 18-34 (19.5%), with the lowest rate among adults ages 65 and older (12.9%).

Women were more likely than men to report frequent fatigue (20% versus 13%).

American Indian and Alaska Native adults had the highest rate of frequent fatigue (25.5%), followed by white adults (18%), Black adults (17.3%) and Hispanic adults (12.9%), with Asian adults having the lowest rate of frequent fatigue (9.1%).
